demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Triggers.value: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
I force myself to think only positive thoughts
I try to push them out of my mind

Threat.value: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something wrong with me as a person
I have to be on guard all the time
The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: Contamination appraisals are hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of accidentally causing serious injury to another person; for this trauma type, guilt, responsibility, danger, or moral failure would be more coherent than feeling physically dirty/contaminated, absent any assault or bodily violation context.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: Other-blame rumination conflicts with the trauma type and the rest of the profile: the central event is that he accidentally injured another person, while the appraisals emphasize defectiveness and threat rather than victimization by others. Dwelling on what other people have done to me points to a different trauma narrative.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Thinking: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
issues.explanation: Magical thinking that the event did not really happen or was not that bad sits awkwardly with the very high-severity profile and with simultaneous endorsement of full sensory reliving plus strong persistent threat and self-defectiveness. Partial minimization can occur, but this item as phrased is in notable tension with the rest of the profile.

vignette: Narayan, an 80-year-old widowed South Asian man who served in the Coast Guard, has been haunted by a traumatic event that occurred decades ago. On a routine rescue mission, he accidentally caused serious injury to another crew member. Since then, Narayan has experienced a complex interplay of symptoms that have progressively worsened over time. Narayan was on duty one stormy evening when the distress call came in. As he navigated through turbulent seas, his mind raced with concern and determination. In an effort to secure a rope, his hand slipped, causing it to strike another crew member in a critical area, resulting in severe injury. The memory of this event is fragmented; pieces of the incident come back to him in disconnected moments that feel completely real across all his senses at once. When he tries to deliberately recall what happened, it becomes difficult to access the full memory. The trauma has left Narayan with intense triggers. Being in a natural environment similar to where the accident occurred, hearing sirens, and talking about the future can all stir up deep distress. For example, when walking near the coast or hearing sirens on his radio, he is immediately transported back to that fateful night. These triggers activate his sense of threat, causing him to feel unsafe in unfamiliar places because he cannot assess the danger effectively. This hypervigilance is a constant presence, as Narayan believes he has to be on guard all the time. Narayan’s self-blame and feelings of being defective exacerbate his distress. He often thinks, “There must be something wrong with me as a person” or that "the event happened because I am the sort of person who makes such mistakes." These negative appraisals lead him to engage in maladaptive strategies like magical thinking, where he tells himself the event did not really happen or was not that bad. He also forces himself to think only positive thoughts and tries to push the memories out of his mind. The cycle is perpetuating itself: when Narayan’s triggers activate his threat response, it intensifies his fragmented and intrusive memories, which in turn reinforce his negative appraisals. These negative beliefs then lead him to engage more heavily in maladaptive strategies like thought suppression and positive reframing. For instance, after hearing sirens near the coast, he tries desperately to push the images out of his mind or tell himself that it was just a routine mission gone wrong. These coping mechanisms only provide temporary relief, often leaving Narayan feeling worse afterward. The more he suppresses thoughts about the event, the harder it becomes for him to recall and process what happened in a healthy manner. He finds himself avoiding unfamiliar places and always choosing where to sit based on how safe or protected he feels, which further isolates him from social activities. The fear of being out in nature or hearing sirens has also affected his occupational environment. As a retiree who volunteers at the Coast Guard once a week, Narayan often avoids outdoor tasks and stays indoors, even if it means missing out on important responsibilities. This avoidance behavior is compounded by his belief that he might cause harm again, leading him to take unnecessary risks in other areas as a form of self-punishment. What frightens Narayan most is the possibility that his guilt will continue to grow and eventually overwhelm him entirely. Despite these struggles, he is hopeful for some relief from his distress. The mounting impact on his daily life finally prompted him to seek help, hoping to break free from this vicious cycle and reclaim a sense of peace and control over his thoughts and actions.
